newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-HEAVY LOSS SIGNALS END OF WINDIES PACE ERA.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-HEAVY LOSS SIGNALS END OF WINDIES PACE ERA.

text.p: For almost 20 years West Indies dominated world cricket with a fearsome four-pronged pace attack, but Tuesday's shattering test series loss to Australia may force a change in the formula.
West Indies captain Courtney Walsh, one of the sharpest prongs in that attack for the past 10 years, admitted the scale of the defeat would cause some soul-searching in his camp.
"I'm very disappointed. It's the first time in my career where there was no chance of having a positive result," a dejected Walsh told reporters after the match.
"It's a performance that you have to look back on and really dig deep to see where we went wrong," he said.

West Indies lost the fourth test by an innings and 183 runs before lunch on the fourth day, their third worst loss of all time and their worst since losing to England at the Oval in 1957 by an innings and 237 runs.
It was also their biggest loss to Australia since the 1930/31 series and handed Australia an unbeatable 3-1 lead in the best-of-five match series.
It also means Australia will retain the Frank Worrell trophy they won in the Caribbean in 1995, when they became the first team to beat West Indies in a series for 15 years.
"Obviously there'll be a lot of discussion when we get back home to try and get the right formula," Walsh said of his first series loss as captain.
Walsh said that, while West Indies had enough fast bowlers to stick with the four-pronged pace attack for now, he was not wedded to the formula.
"I'm not saying it should be a god-given thing that you always have four fast bowlers, but I know we have four good enough fast bowlers to do the job," he said.
The tall, 34-year-old Jamaican said the loss just before the Adelaide test of pace bowler Curtly Ambrose, the chief destroyer in their third test victory, was a key factor.

The fourth prong in the current team, Kenneth Benjamin, was also out with injury and Walsh was forced to draft in two newcomers, Cameron Cuffy and Patterson Thompson, to support himself and Ian Bishop.
But critics point to the average age of the current four-prong attack of 31 and the lack of obvious successors as reasons for a formula change.
Victorious captain Mark Taylor, who became the first Australia captain to win two successive series against West Indies, said the tourists must re-examine their pace formula.
"To be a good cricket team in the current environment, you need to have variety and that's something the West Indies haven't got," Taylor said.
"The West Indies have had a formula now since about the late 1970s of picking four quick bowlers and being able to continually beat sides with that.

"But in 1995 we conquered that and I think we proved in this series we can conquer that again, so either they've got to stick to that formula and continue to improve their fast bowlers or make a change to that formula," he said.
Taylor said Australia would never play a test match with only four fast bowlers while he was captain and that a varied attack with quality spin bowlers were crucial elements in his team's success.

That was never more evident than in this match, where leg-spinners Shane Warne and Michael Bevan took 16 wickets between them, humbling a West Indies batting line-up that seemed unable to understand their pace, guile and flight.
The two teams now travel to Perth for the anti-climactic fifth and final test.
